notes.definition: Cell differentiation is the process by which a cell changes to become specialised for a particular function, acquiring the sub-cellular structures it needs to carry out that function.
explanation: Every multicellular organism starts life as a single cell, a fertilised egg. This cell divides again and again to make many cells. At first these cells are all similar and unspecialised. As the organism develops, the cells differentiate: they change to form different types of cells, such as nerve cells, muscle cells and blood cells in animals, or xylem, phloem and root hair cells in plants.

As a cell differentiates, it acquires different sub-cellular structures that enable it to carry out a certain function. It has then become a specialised cell. For example, a cell that differentiates into a muscle cell develops many mitochondria and protein fibres that can contract. A cell that becomes a palisade cell in a leaf develops many chloroplasts. A cell that becomes a xylem cell develops thick walls strengthened with lignin, then dies and loses its end walls to form a hollow tube.

Animals and plants differ in when their cells differentiate. Most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage of development, mainly in the embryo. Once an animal is mature, cell division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement: for example, making new skin cells to heal a cut or replacing red blood cells and the cells lining the gut as they wear out. Specialised animal cells cannot usually turn into a different type of cell.

In contrast, many types of plant cell keep the ability to differentiate throughout the life of the plant. Plants have regions called meristems at the tips of their shoots and roots, where cells keep dividing and can differentiate into any type of plant cell. This is why plants keep growing all their lives, and why a gardener can grow a whole new plant from a small cutting: cells in the cutting differentiate to form new roots.

Cell differentiation is important because it allows a multicellular organism to have many different types of specialised cell. Specialised cells group together to form tissues, tissues form organs and organs form organ systems. Each type of cell is adapted to do one job very well, so the organism as a whole works much more efficiently than if every cell had to do every job. Differentiation is what makes large, complex organisms possible.
keyFacts: Differentiation is the process by which cells become specialised.
As an organism develops, cells differentiate to form different types of cells.
As a cell differentiates, it acquires different sub-cellular structures to carry out a certain function.
Most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage of development.
Many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.
In mature animals, cell division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.
Plants have meristems at shoot and root tips where cells keep dividing and differentiating.
Differentiation allows specialised cells to form tissues, organs and organ systems.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which a cell becomes specialised to carry out a particular function.
A cell that has acquired sub-cellular structures and features that adapt it for a particular function.
A cell that has not yet differentiated and so does not yet have a particular function.
An early stage of development of an organism, when most animal cells differentiate.
Tissue at the tips of plant shoots and roots where cells keep dividing and can differentiate into any type of plant cell.
The main purposes of cell division in mature animals: healing damaged tissue and replacing worn-out cells.
A group of cells with a similar structure and function working together.

workedExamples.title: Predicting how a cell changes as it differentiates
workedExamples.question: An unspecialised cell in a young leaf differentiates into a palisade cell, which carries out most of the photosynthesis in the leaf. Suggest one sub-cellular structure the cell acquires in large numbers and explain why.
steps: Recall which sub-cellular structure carries out that process: chloroplasts.
Link the structure to the function: more chloroplasts means more light absorbed and more photosynthesis.
workedExamples.answer: Many chloroplasts, because chloroplasts contain chlorophyll to absorb light and are where photosynthesis takes place.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a difference between plants and animals
workedExamples.question: A gardener grows a new plant from a short piece of stem. Explain why the same cannot be done with a piece of a human arm.
steps: Plants: many plant cells retain the ability to differentiate throughout life, so cells in the stem can differentiate into root cells.
Animals: most animal cells differentiate at an early stage; in adults, cell division is mainly for repair and replacement.
So human arm cells cannot differentiate into all the new cell types needed to make a whole organism.
workedExamples.answer: Plant stem cells can still differentiate into new types of cell such as roots, but most human cells differentiated early in development and can no longer form new types of cell.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that differentiation and cell division are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact cell division makes more cells, while differentiation is the process of a cell changing to become specialised. A cell may divide many times before it differentiates.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think adult animals make lots of new types of cell all the time.
misconceptions.right: In fact most animal cells differentiate early in development. In mature animals, cell division is mainly for repair and replacement of cells of the same types.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plant cells stop differentiating when the plant is fully grown.
misconceptions.right: In fact many types of plant cell keep the ability to differentiate throughout life, which is why plants can keep growing and can be grown from cuttings.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a specialised cell has different genes from other body cells.
misconceptions.right: In fact the body cells of an organism contain the same genetic material. Differentiation changes the structures a cell develops, not which genetic material it carries.

realWorld: Gardeners and plant growers take cuttings from a parent plant; cells in the cutting differentiate to form new roots, producing many identical plants cheaply.
When you cut your skin, cell division in the surrounding tissue produces new skin cells to repair the wound, an example of division for repair in a mature animal.

Because most human cells cannot differentiate into other types, damage to tissues like the spinal cord or heart muscle is hard to repair, which is why scientists research ways of producing new specialised cells.
examTips: Use the phrase 'acquires different sub-cellular structures' when describing what happens as a cell differentiates. It is the key idea in the specification.
Learn the contrast: animal cells differentiate at an early stage; many plant cells retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.
If asked what cell division is for in adult animals, say 'repair and replacement', not 'growth'.
To explain the importance of differentiation, link specialised cells to forming tissues, organs and organ systems, and to the organism working efficiently.

When asked to suggest how a cell changes during differentiation, think about its function first, then pick the structure that carries out that function (e.g. mitochondria for energy, chloroplasts for photosynthesis).
summary: Differentiation is how cells become specialised.
A differentiating cell acquires sub-cellular structures for its function.
Most animal cells differentiate early in development.
Many plant cells can differentiate throughout life (meristems).
In mature animals, cell division is mainly for repair and replacement.
Differentiation allows tissues, organs and organ systems to form, so organisms work efficiently.

flashcards.back: The process by which a cell becomes specialised for a particular function.

flashcards.front: What does a cell acquire as it differentiates?
flashcards.back: Different sub-cellular structures that enable it to carry out a certain function.

flashcards.front: When do most animal cells differentiate?
flashcards.back: At an early stage of development (in the embryo).

flashcards.front: Can plant cells differentiate in a mature plant?
flashcards.back: Yes. Many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.

flashcards.front: What is cell division mainly for in mature animals?

flashcards.back: A region at shoot and root tips where plant cells keep dividing and can differentiate into any type of plant cell.

flashcards.front: Why can a new plant be grown from a cutting?
flashcards.back: Cells in the cutting can still differentiate, for example into root cells.
It produces specialised cells that form tissues, organs and organ systems, so the organism works efficiently.

flashcards.front: What structure would a cell differentiating into a muscle cell gain in large numbers?
What structure would a cell differentiating into a palisade cell gain in large numbers?
Is differentiation the same as cell division?
flashcards.back: No. Division makes more cells; differentiation makes a cell specialised.

questions.question: What is meant by cell differentiation?
options: The division of a cell into two identical cells
The process by which a cell becomes specialised for a particular function
The movement of substances into a cell
The death of old, worn-out cells
markScheme: 1 mark: the process by which a cell becomes specialised for a particular function
questions.explanation: Differentiation is about cells becoming specialised. Cell division produces more cells, but that is a different process.

questions.question: When do most types of animal cell differentiate?
options: At an early stage of development
Only in old age
Continuously throughout life
Only after the animal is fully grown
markScheme: 1 mark: at an early stage of development
questions.explanation: Most animal cells differentiate early, mainly in the embryo. It is many plant cells, not animal cells, that keep the ability to differentiate throughout life.

questions.question: In mature animals, what is cell division mainly used for?
options: Making new types of specialised cell
Growing new limbs
Producing chloroplasts
Repair and replacement of cells
markScheme: 1 mark: repair and replacement of cells
questions.explanation: Adult animals mainly divide cells to repair damage (such as a cut) and replace worn-out cells. They cannot regrow limbs, and animal cells never have chloroplasts.

questions.question: In which group of organisms do many types of cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life?
options: Humans
Fish
Plants
Birds
markScheme: 1 mark: plants
questions.explanation: Many plant cells, especially in meristems, can differentiate throughout life. Humans, fish and birds are animals, whose cells mostly differentiate early in development.

questions.question: Which statement describes what happens to a cell as it differentiates?
options: It acquires different sub-cellular structures so it can carry out a certain function
It loses all of its genetic material
It becomes a prokaryotic cell
It always develops a cell wall
markScheme: 1 mark: it acquires different sub-cellular structures so it can carry out a certain function
questions.explanation: Differentiating cells gain the structures they need for their function. They remain eukaryotic, and animal cells never develop cell walls.

questions.question: A cell differentiates into a muscle cell. Which sub-cellular structure is it likely to gain in large numbers?
options: Chloroplasts
Mitochondria
Cell wall
Plasmids
markScheme: 1 mark: mitochondria
questions.explanation: Muscle cells need lots of energy for contraction, released by aerobic respiration in mitochondria. Chloroplasts and cell walls are plant features, and plasmids are found in bacteria.

questions.question: A gardener can grow a whole new plant from a small cutting of stem. What is the best explanation?
options: Plant cells do not need to divide to grow
Cuttings contain seeds
Plant cells have no genetic material
Many plant cells keep the ability to differentiate throughout life
markScheme: 1 mark: many plant cells keep the ability to differentiate throughout life
questions.explanation: Cells in the cutting can still differentiate into new cell types, such as root cells. Plant cells do divide to grow, cuttings do not contain seeds and all plant cells have genetic material.

questions.question: Which is an example of cell division for replacement in an adult human?
options: Growing a new arm after one is lost
Forming a new heart
Replacing skin cells that are worn away
Producing chloroplasts in skin cells
markScheme: 1 mark: replacing skin cells that are worn away
questions.explanation: Adult humans divide cells to replace cells of the same type, such as skin cells. They cannot grow new limbs or organs, and human cells never contain chloroplasts.

questions.question: Why is cell differentiation important for a multicellular organism?
options: It makes all cells identical so they can share every task
It produces specialised cells that form tissues, organs and organ systems, each carrying out different functions efficiently
It stops cells from ever dividing again
It allows every cell in the organism to photosynthesise
markScheme: 1 mark: it produces specialised cells that form tissues, organs and organ systems, each carrying out different functions efficiently
questions.explanation: Differentiation makes cells different, not identical, so each type can be adapted to a job. Differentiated cells can still divide for repair, and only some plant cells photosynthesise.

questions.question: Which observation best supports the statement 'many plant cells retain the ability to differentiate throughout life'?
options: A piece of stem from a mature plant, placed in water, grows new roots
Human skin heals after a cut
Leaves change colour in autumn
A human embryo develops a heart
markScheme: 1 mark: a piece of stem from a mature plant, placed in water, grows new roots
questions.explanation: Stem cells forming root cells shows a mature plant's cells differentiating into a new type. Skin healing and embryo development are about animals, and leaf colour change does not involve forming new cell types.

questions.question: State what is meant by a specialised cell.
acceptedAnswers: has features for a particular job
markScheme: 1 mark: a cell that is adapted / has structures to carry out a particular function
questions.explanation: A specialised cell has differentiated and acquired the sub-cellular structures it needs for one particular job.

questions.question: Give one reason why cells divide in a mature animal.
markScheme: 1 mark: repair (of damaged tissue) or replacement (of worn-out cells)
questions.explanation: In mature animals, cell division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.

questions.question: Name the type of organism in which many cells can differentiate throughout life.
markScheme: 1 mark: plants
questions.explanation: Many plant cells retain the ability to differentiate throughout life, particularly in meristems.

questions.question: Describe what happens to a cell as it differentiates.
markScheme: 1 mark: it acquires different sub-cellular structures
1 mark: so it becomes specialised to carry out a certain function
questions.explanation: Differentiation means gaining the structures needed for a specific job, turning an unspecialised cell into a specialised one.

questions.question: Compare when cell differentiation happens in animals and in plants.
markScheme: 1 mark: most animal cells differentiate at an early stage (of development)
1 mark: many plant cells can differentiate throughout life
questions.explanation: A comparison needs both sides: animals early, plants throughout life.

questions.question: An unspecialised cell near the tip of a root differentiates into a root hair cell. Suggest two changes to the structure of the cell.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: grows a long extension / root hair (large surface area); gains more mitochondria; develops a large permanent vacuole; does not develop chloroplasts
questions.explanation: The cell develops features suited to absorbing water and mineral ions: a long hair for surface area and many mitochondria to release energy for active transport.

questions.question: Explain how a cut on your finger is able to heal.
markScheme: 1 mark: cells near the cut divide (by mitosis) to produce new cells
1 mark: the new cells repair / replace the damaged tissue
questions.explanation: In mature animals, cell division is mainly for repair and replacement. Cells next to the wound divide to make new cells of the same type to fill the gap.

questions.question: A sperm cell develops from an unspecialised cell. Suggest how the sub-cellular structures of the cell change as it differentiates, and explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: gains many mitochondria (in the mid-piece) to release energy
1 mark: develops a tail so it can swim (to the egg)
1 mark: develops an acrosome containing enzymes to digest a way into the egg
questions.explanation: Each new structure links to the sperm cell's function of reaching and fertilising an egg. This shows that differentiation means acquiring the sub-cellular structures needed for a function.

questions.question: A tree can grow a new branch where an old one has been cut off, but a human cannot grow a new finger. Explain this difference.
markScheme: 1 mark: many plant cells (in meristems) keep the ability to differentiate throughout life
1 mark: so the tree can produce all the cell types needed for a new branch
1 mark: most human cells differentiated early in development / in adults division is only for repair and replacement, so new types of cell for a finger cannot be made
questions.explanation: The difference comes down to when cells can differentiate. Plants keep this ability, while adult human cell division only repairs and replaces existing cell types.

questions.question: A bacterium is a single-celled organism. Explain why a bacterium does not need cell differentiation, but a human does.
acceptedAnswers: single cell carries out all life processes
markScheme: 1 mark: the single bacterial cell must carry out all life processes itself
1 mark: a human is multicellular, so different cells can carry out different functions
1 mark: differentiation produces specialised cells forming tissues / organs / organ systems, so the body works efficiently
questions.explanation: A single cell cannot divide up jobs, so specialisation has no purpose. In a large multicellular organism, differentiated cells form tissues and organs that share out functions efficiently.

questions.question: Explain why cell differentiation is important to multicellular organisms, and compare cell differentiation in animals and plants.
markScheme: Indicative content:
a multicellular organism develops from a single fertilised egg
cells divide, then differentiate to form different types of cell
as a cell differentiates it acquires different sub-cellular structures
it becomes specialised to carry out a particular function
specialised cells form tissues, organs and organ systems
so the organism carries out its functions efficiently / can be large and complex
most animal cells differentiate at an early stage of development
in mature animals cell division is mainly for repair and replacement
many plant cells retain the ability to differentiate throughout life
plants have meristems at shoot and root tips / plants can grow throughout life / can be grown from cuttings
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear explanation of the importance of differentiation and a detailed comparison of animals and plants.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some explanation of importance and at least one valid comparison between animals and plants.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about differentiation or about animals or plants, with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A full answer has two parts: why differentiation matters (specialised cells, tissues, organs, efficiency) and how it differs (animal cells early; plant cells throughout life; adult animal division for repair and replacement).

questions.question: Describe how a fertilised egg develops into an organism that contains many different types of specialised cell.
markScheme: Indicative content:
the fertilised egg divides many times
to form an embryo of unspecialised cells
cells then differentiate as the organism develops
they acquire different sub-cellular structures
becoming specialised cells such as nerve, muscle or blood cells
similar specialised cells group together to form tissues
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear sequence from cell division to differentiation to specialised cells, mentioning sub-cellular structures.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): mentions division or specialisation without a clear sequence.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key sequence is division to make many cells, then differentiation where cells acquire different sub-cellular structures and become specialised.

questions.question: Specialised cells with a similar structure and function group together. What do they form?
options: Plasmids
Chromosomes
Tissues
Ribosomes
markScheme: 1 mark: tissues
questions.explanation: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together. Plasmids, chromosomes and ribosomes are structures inside cells.

questions.question: A cell in a young leaf differentiates into a palisade cell, which carries out most of the leaf's photosynthesis. Which structure does it gain in large numbers?
options: Plasmids
Lignin rings
Acrosomes
Chloroplasts
markScheme: 1 mark: chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are where photosynthesis takes place. Lignin rings are found in xylem, acrosomes in sperm cells and plasmids in bacteria.

questions.question: Give one example of a specialised plant cell formed by differentiation.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one from: root hair cell; xylem cell; phloem cell; palisade cell; guard cell
questions.explanation: Root hair, xylem and phloem cells are the plant examples named in the specification; other correct specialised plant cells are also accepted.

questions.question: Suggest why it is useful to a plant that cells at the tips of its shoots and roots can still differentiate.
markScheme: 1 mark: the plant can keep growing throughout its life
1 mark: producing new types of cell, e.g. for new leaves / roots / to replace parts that are eaten or damaged
questions.explanation: Meristems let a plant keep adding new leaves, stems and roots and replace damaged parts. Plants cannot move, so continued growth lets them reach new light, water and mineral ions.

questions.question: Which statement about differentiation is correct?
options: Most plant cells differentiate early, but animal cells can differentiate throughout life
Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage, but many plant cells can differentiate throughout life
Neither animal nor plant cells can differentiate after the embryo stage
Differentiated animal cells can easily turn into any other type of cell
markScheme: 1 mark: most animal cells differentiate at an early stage, but many plant cells can differentiate throughout life
questions.explanation: The first option reverses plants and animals. Plant cells in meristems differentiate throughout life, and differentiated animal cells generally cannot change into other cell types.
